findings.title: Device-limit denial is cached as success
findings.body: tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice, and a cache hit returns nil without touching the database. The cache TTL is 29 minutes and the entry is not removed when tagging fails. Authenticate now treats a nil TagDevice result as success and only denies access for ErrDeviceLimitReached. So the first request from a new device over the limit is rejected, but that rejection is stored as a successful cache entry. Every later request for that device id skips the limit check and is issued an anonymous identity, and the device is never inserted, so it never consumes a slot. A concurrent request can also observe the cache entry and be authenticated before the first request's limit check finishes. After one denial, the cap does not apply to that client for the rest of the TTL, on every instance that has seen it.

findings.title: Device limit does not actually gate anonymous access
findings.body: The new access check only denies authentication when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate then still returns an anonymous identity, when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent or when web.RemoteAddr cannot be parsed as an IP. Existing tests show client IP is taken from X-Forwarded-For, so a non-IP forwarded-for value forces the parse-failure path even if a device id is sent. Any other tagging error is only logged in client.go and authentication continues, so a request that makes the insert fail is granted access and is not counted. The device id is also chosen by the client, so many users can send one already-accepted id and all pass the update path while occupying a single slot. Omitting the header is enough to use anonymous access with no limit check at all. As written, device_limit does not bound anonymous access.

findings.title: Device limit check and insert are not atomic
findings.body: When device_limit is positive, CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one WithDbSession and, if the count is under the limit, inserts in a second WithDbSession. Nothing wraps the two statements in a transaction or takes a lock, and the unique key is only on device_id, so it does not cap the number of rows. Concurrent anonymous requests that all observe count < limit will all insert. With 50 simultaneous new device ids and a limit of 10, all 50 can commit and the table stays at 50; nothing rolls the extras back. That is the multi-instance, multi-user load this cap is meant to control, so AnonymousDeviceLimit is not a hard limit.

findings.title: Provider signature change breaks Wire startup
findings.body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer takes an anonstore.AnonStore and now requires db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a bare int64 device-limit argument. Grafana builds the server with Google Wire and commits pkg/server/wire_gen.go; this PR does not update wire.go or wire_gen.go, and the only updated call sites are tests. The generated injector still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile. Regenerating Wire also cannot satisfy a raw int64, so ProvideAnonDBStore has to be dropped from the provider set (it is now called internally) or the limit must be injected via *setting.Cfg. Until that is done the binary does not build.

findings.title: Anonymous auth now waits on the database even when the limit is off
findings.body: Device tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and did not block login. Authenticate now calls TagDevice on the request path for every anonymous authentication, including when device_limit is 0, which disables enforcement. A local-cache miss waits for a database write before an identity is returned; a non-zero limit adds a COUNT(*) first, and that count is not cached. The cache is per process, so each instance repeats the work. A slow database delays every new anonymous session, and because the call is synchronous an unauthenticated client can force a count-and-write per request by rotating X-Grafana-Device-Id. Previously that work could not stall the request.

findings.title: Limit tests never cover the allow-existing or auth paths
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only inserts one device and asserts that a second new device id returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. It never checks the behavior the new branch claims: an already-registered device must still be updated and accepted once the count is at the limit. A broken updateDevice WHERE clause that rejects every device, including known ones, would still pass. Nothing at the AnonDeviceService or Anonymous.Authenticate level covers the limit either, so the 29-minute cache treating a failed tag as success, and a missing device-id header still receiving an anonymous identity, are both untested. The new test runs on SQLite only, so MySQL/Postgres placeholder or rows-affected differences in the new UPDATE are not exercised.

findings.title: device_limit is undocumented and 0 means unlimited
findings.body: auth.anonymous.device_limit is read with MustInt64(0) but conf/defaults.ini and the configure-grafana docs are not updated. Operators discover settings from defaults.ini, and generated config docs come from that file, so the new cap is invisible. The code treats 0 as 'do not enforce' rather than 'allow zero devices', and that is not stated anywhere a user will see it. Setting device_limit = 0 to try to disallow anonymous devices silently leaves the limit disabled.
